text: In 1932, Australia sent soldiers with machine guns to fight a war.
The enemy? About 20,000 emus. Give or take.
Six feet tall. 50 km an hour. Zero fear.
History calls it the Great Emu War.
Except it wasn't a war. Nobody ever declared anything.
It was pest control. With machine guns. And the emus? They won.
Our story starts after the First World War.
Thousands of soldiers were coming home. Now what?
The government had an idea. Give them land. Lots of land.
In Western Australia. Far away. Very dry. Very empty.
Grow wheat, they said. It'll be great, they said.
Then the Great Depression hit, and wheat prices crashed.
The government promised to help. The help did not arrive.
So the farmers were broke, tired, and very much alone.
Then, in late 1932, some visitors showed up.
And the emus were fine.
After breeding season, emus head west, toward the coast.
This year, they found something new on the way.
Fresh wheat. Fresh water. And very convenient fences.
They ate the crops. They drank the water.
And they flattened the fences, letting the rabbits in too.
The farmers, many of them ex-soldiers, had a suggestion.
"We know how to fix this. Machine guns."
They took it to the Defence Minister, George Pearce.
"Sure. Why not."
Some say he liked the publicity. Others, the target practice.
Enter Major G.P.W. Meredith, Royal Australian Artillery.
He brought two soldiers, two Lewis guns, and 10,000 bullets.
The deal: the army brings the guns. The farmers pay for the bullets.
The start was delayed. By rain. Which the emus enjoyed.
On 2 November 1932, the operation began.
First sighting: about 50 emus. Way out of range.
Local farmers tried to herd them into an ambush.
The emus split into small groups and ran in every direction.
Which made them almost impossible to hit.
A few were hit. The rest? The emus were fine.
Two days later, Meredith set up an ambush at a dam.
Around 1,000 emus walked straight toward the guns.
Perfect. The soldiers waited until they were close.
Then they opened fire.
About 12 emus went down.
And then the gun jammed.
The rest of the flock was gone before it could be fixed.
Meredith tried a new idea. Put the gun on a truck.
The truck couldn't catch the emus. The ground was too rough.
The gunner couldn't aim. He could barely hold on.
Then one emu got tangled in the steering, and the truck crashed.
Into a fence. Which, to be fair, was already broken.
An ornithologist later joked that the emus used guerrilla tactics.
Every group had one tall lookout, keeping watch.
Back home, the newspapers were having a wonderful time.
Parliament started asking questions. Awkward ones.
On 8 November, the army pulled out.
About 2,500 rounds fired. Emus killed? Accounts disagree, wildly.
But the emus kept coming. And the farmers kept complaining.
The state's premier asked for the soldiers to come back.
On 13 November, Meredith returned. Round two.
This time, it went better. Sort of.
By early December, around 100 emus a week.
Meredith claimed 986 kills, using nearly 10,000 bullets.
That's about 10 bullets per emu.
He also claimed thousands more were wounded. Historians are not so sure.
And then, Meredith said something remarkable about his enemy.
"If we had a military division with the bullet-carrying capacity of these birds,
it would face any army in the world."
On 10 December, the army left. For good.
So, who won? Well, the emus were still there.
What actually worked? Paying farmers a bounty for every emu.
In 1934, over 57,000 bounties were claimed in six months.
Later, huge barrier fences went up to keep the emus out.
So no, it wasn't really a war. Nobody declared it.
It was a cull, carried out by soldiers, that mostly failed.
The name stuck, because, honestly, it is just too good.
Today, the emu is on Australia's coat of arms.
Major Meredith became a very funny footnote in history.
And what about the emus?
The emus were fine.
